title: Mission Control
tagline: Your induction. Your codename. Your first badges.
objectives: I can keep my account safe: I know what makes a password hard to guess, and why I never share mine.
I know the rules of the DT rooms and what to do when something goes wrong.
I can find my way around this website, and I know where my work is saved so it follows me to any computer.

config.headline: Welcome to Digital Technology.
lines: You have seventeen Digital Technology lessons this year, one every fortnight.

You will start by writing code — telling a small computer what to do, and watching it do it. After that you will open a computer up and find out what each part is for, discover how photographs and music are stored as nothing but numbers, follow a message across a network, and design something of your own.

The screen you just came from is called MISSION CONTROL. It is your home page for the whole year: every one of the seventeen lessons sits on it, and you come back to it at the start and the end of every lesson.

Today is the lesson that gets you set up, so that none of the other sixteen have to stop and explain things. By the end of the hour you will be able to log in on your own, keep your account safe, find your way around Mission Control, and know exactly where your work is saved.

You collect badges as you go — five of them today, one for each main part — and points called XP. They are simply a record of what you have done — they unlock new colours for this website later in the year, and only you and your teacher can see them. Nobody is ranked against anybody.
config.help: This screen is only for reading — the website is introducing the year and today's lesson. Nothing to answer. When the writing finishes, a button appears at the bottom — press it to start. No button yet means the writing hasn't finished.

chunks.title: Badge 1 — Your Account and the Rules

config.intro: In this part you will learn how to keep your school account safe — what makes a password hard for someone else to guess, why yours stays yours, and why you sign out every time. Then the rules of this room. Three things to read, then some questions.

steps.title: Your password is the one thing you never share
steps.text: Not with your best friend, not with your sister, not with anyone who says they are helping. You never type it where somebody can see the keys, and you never write it in a file on the computer. If you think somebody knows it, tell a teacher and change it — you are not in trouble for saying so.
steps.confirm: I understand my password is only for me

steps.title: What makes a password hard to guess
steps.text: Two things: LENGTH and SURPRISE. Three unusual words stuck together, with a capital letter and a number or a symbol, is far stronger than one short clever one. Maple!Harbour6sky would take years to break. What gets guessed first is always the same handful of things: your name, your birthday, your team, the word password with numbers on the end, and runs of keys like qwerty. Newry2013 falls in seconds.
steps.confirm: I can see what makes a password hard to guess

steps.title: Sign out — every time
steps.text: When you finish on ANY school computer, sign out. It locks your files and your privacy behind you. Staying logged in is like walking off and leaving your locker wide open — and anything anyone does in your account looks like YOU did it.
steps.confirm: I'll sign out every time I finish

Read it once more slowly, then put your hand up.

config.intro: In this part you will learn your way around this website, so you never have to ask where something is. A light moves around the screen and stops on each part in turn. Read each one, then press Next.

stops.title: The lesson board
stops.text: Your whole year, at a glance. All seventeen Digital Technology lessons live on this board, in the order you will do them. This is where you start every lesson.

stops.title: Locks
stops.text: A padlock means 'not yet'. Your teacher opens each lesson when the class gets to it. A lesson you have finished never locks again — you can go back into it any time, from any computer.

stops.title: Your record
stops.text: Your badges, your points, and the ring showing how far through the year you are. This is private: only you and your teacher can see it. There is no class scoreboard here.

stops.title: The ? button
stops.text: Stuck? The round ? in the corner is always there, on every screen, all year. It will not tell you the answer. It tells you the order to try things in — and your teacher is the last step of that order, so put your hand up.

config.intro: In this part you will learn where school work should be kept, and why it matters — and you will find out what it is like to work on the same thing as somebody else at the very same moment. Six files have landed in your Inbox. Send each one where it really belongs — and if something should never be saved at all, there is a place for that too. Choose wrong and the file comes straight back to you, and you are NOT told the answer — work it out from what each file actually is.
config.pairPrompt: YOU ARE WORKING IN A PAIR. You and the person beside you are on this together. Agree before either of you lets a file go — say out loud why it belongs there — and only then drop it. If you disagree, talk it out; you get one shot at each file.
config.channelPrompt: YOU ARE ABOUT TO BE PAIRED WITH SOMEONE ELSE IN THIS CLASS. She will be sitting at a different computer, looking at this same Vault, at the same moment as you. The website will give her a temporary code name for this Vault — you will see it at the top of the screen, and you will find out who she really was when the Vault is sealed. Only one of you holds the controls at a time, and the screen tells you whose turn it is. Use the message box to agree BEFORE a file is dropped — say why it belongs there — then whoever holds the controls drops it. You get one shot at each file, so agree first. (If your class has an odd number, the last three pupils share one Vault as a three.)

debrief.sync: Freeze. You and your partner just worked on the SAME thing at the SAME moment, agreeing every move — like a video call: everyone there together, reacting live. Computing's name for working-together-live is SYNCHRONOUS (say: SINK-ron-us — 'at the same time').
debrief.syncLive: Freeze. Think about what just happened: you and your partner were on DIFFERENT machines, yet you worked on the SAME Vault at the SAME moment — every message appearing on the other screen moments after it was sent, every drop showing up on both screens moments later. Computing's name for working-together-live is SYNCHRONOUS (say: SINK-ron-us — 'at the same time'). You didn't just learn the word — you just DID it, over the school network.
debrief.syncCatchup: In class this is a job for two: two pupils, two computers, one shared Vault — agreeing every move at the same moment over a live channel, like a video call. Computing's name for working together live is SYNCHRONOUS (say: SINK-ron-us — 'at the same time'). You have just proved the solo version works too.
debrief.async: Now think of sending a message tonight that your friend doesn't read until tomorrow. You were never together — but the work still moved, because it waited in a shared place. That's ASYNCHRONOUS ('NOT at the same time'). Your Drive does both: work on something live with a classmate, or leave it waiting for future-you to open — even at home. You'll use both all year.

config.help: Drag each file from the Inbox into the folder you both agree it belongs in. Talk in the message box FIRST — only the pupil at the controls can drag, and the screen always says whose turn it is. A file that bounces back was wrong: talk it through and try another. The website never gives the answer — working it out together is the activity.

config.intro: The Vault you just filed was a pretend one. Now the real thing.

steps.title: Open your real Drive
steps.text: Open a NEW tab and go to drive.google.com — on a school computer it signs you in by itself. That page is YOUR real Vault: it follows your login to any device, even at home.
steps.confirm: I can see my Google Drive

steps.title: Spot the + New button
steps.text: Top-left: the + New button. That is how folders get made — but you are NOT making any today. Your only job in this step is to FIND the button and remember where it lives. Making the folders is a whole activity of its own called Files That Follow You — a side quest, one of the short extra lessons on your lesson board — and in it you will build your real folders right here: School, DT Work, the lot.

config.help: Nothing is built today — you are only FINDING things. Open a new tab, go to drive.google.com, find what the step asks for, then come back to this tab and press the tick. If the new tab didn't sign you in, put your hand up.

config.intro: This badge is different from the others: there is nothing new to learn in it. You are going to be asked sixteen quick questions about computers, to find out what you can already do and what is brand new to you — before any of it has been taught. This is not a test and you cannot fail it. It is a snapshot of what you already know, so that in June you and your teacher can both see how far you have come. Answer on your own, no conferring. You will NOT be told right or wrong on these — after each answer you will see 'Answer saved', which means your answer went in safely.

belonging.title: One last thing, before you go
lines: Before you go — one thing everybody starting this subject needs to hear.

In your first few weeks here, some of it will feel hard. Logins will fail. Code will break. Files will hide. That is not a sign you are bad at this. It is what learning technology feels like for EVERYONE — including every pupil who sat where you are sitting, and every adult in this building.
The feeling is normal and it does not last. The people who keep going find that the thing that felt impossible in September feels easy by June.
You belong in this room and you belong in this subject.

config.help: Press Shuffle until a codename appears that you like, then press Keep this name. After that, read the five promises and sign at the bottom — signing means you agree to keep them.
